scenes.title: An open day in three weeks
scenes.description: Maya is answering emails at the community centre when her manager, Rosa, asks her to organise an open day in three weeks. By lunch Maya has a long list: book rooms, call volunteers, write the newsletter, and the emails are still waiting.

scenes.title: Leo suggests a chat tool
scenes.description: Her colleague Leo sees the list and shows her an AI chat tool on his phone. Examples such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot appear as names, and most have a free version.

scenes.title: A polished first draft
scenes.description: Maya types a request into a generic AI chat tool and a warm, professional paragraph appears in seconds. Her finger hovers over Copy.

scenes.title: Is confident enough?
scenes.description: The scene pauses and asks the learner whether an answer that sounds this confident is enough to trust.

scenes.title: Fifty years?
scenes.description: Maya rereads the draft and spots a claim that the centre has served the community for over fifty years. An animation shows the tool choosing likely next words rather than checking facts.

scenes.title: Draft first, then check
scenes.description: Maya keeps the parts she likes and adds a note to check the opening date with Rosa. The learner is invited to think of something to ask a chat tool this week and one detail they would check.

cues.text: Remember Maya from Module 1?
She runs the office at a busy community centre.
This morning, she’s halfway through answering emails when her manager, Rosa, stops by her desk.
“We’re holding an open day,” Rosa says.
“Could you organise it?”
“Of course. When is it?”
“Three weeks from Saturday.”
“Three weeks?”
By lunch, Maya’s made a list.
Book the rooms.
Call the volunteers.
Get something into the newsletter.
And she still has those emails to answer.
Her colleague Leo sees the list.
“Why don’t you try an AI chat tool for the newsletter?”
He pulls out his phone.
“There’s ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot.
Most have a free version.
Just ask for what you need, like you’d ask me.”
So Maya types, “Write a short, welcoming paragraph about our community centre for the open day newsletter.”
A few seconds later, there it is.
It’s warm.
It sounds professional.
Maya can already picture it in the newsletter.
“I could actually use this.”
Her finger hovers over Copy.
Before Maya pastes it in, what do you think?
If an answer sounds this confident, is that enough to trust what it says?
When Maya reads it again, one line catches her eye.
“For over fifty years, our centre has brought people together.”
“Fifty years? Where did it get that from?”
An AI writes by predicting which words are most likely to come next, based on patterns it learned from an enormous amount of text.
That is why its writing flows so smoothly.
It has seen millions of well-written paragraphs.
But it is not checking facts as it goes.
It is choosing words that sound right.
So it can sound exactly as confident when it is wrong as when it is right.
A line about serving the community for fifty years fits the kind of newsletter Maya asked for.
To know whether it’s true, she needs to check when the centre actually opened.
So she keeps the parts she likes and puts a note next to that line.
“Check opening date with Rosa before printing.”
That’s the habit we’ll practise in this module.
Let AI help you get a first draft.
Before you use it, check the details someone else might rely on.
Now it’s your turn.
Think of one thing you could ask an AI chat tool to help with this week.
Maybe a message, a short description, or a list of ideas.
What’s one detail you’d check before using the answer?
